doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
title: Lodge band, choosing the clarinet and teacher Mr. List
summary: A Bronx lodge band recruiter offered him instruments and he chose clarinet inspired by Shaw and Goodman; Mr. List taught him fingerings.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: So I did that, and I don’t remember particularly performing as performing, but I was taking these lessons, you know, maybe a couple of years of once a week or once every two weeks you know. And I did it and I don’t know what it cost but they had to pay money you know. And my father was not making a lot of money, it was Depression times you know. And then my father belonged to a lodge in the Bronx. We lived in the Bronx. And they had a band, a small band. And they were looking for recruits. So — what was her name, there was a little Eva or Emma, something or other. And they were Hungarians you know. And she cornered me and said what did I want to play — would I like to join the band. I said well —. She said, “what would you like to play, the tuba?” You know.
Yeah they needed a tuba, right?

Yeah, like that. I said no. I never thought of it. No, no, no. She said well trumpet? And she said clarinet? And you know I must have been pretty hip already or something, but I immediately thought of Artie Shaw or Benny Goodman. “Yeah, the clarinet.” It’s very funny you know. And Woody Herman. I knew Woody Herman a little and I told him this story. And I said you’re one of the guys responsible. Matter of fact I told Benny Goodman too. You’re one of the guys responsible for me.

And I met Artie Shaw, I knew Artie Shaw a little you know. I never told him but I believe with that sort of thing you’ve got to tell people. So it was clarinet. And her name was List, I forget his first name, Mr. List I called him. Very nice man. He was sort of like the violin teacher , slight, pale, very musical. I don’t know what he played. But he was a very good teacher in that he taught me fingerings. I mean to this day, you know, the high notes and everything. You know like really correct. The alternates, and how to get around. As a matter of fact I remember, this is very funny, that I played the Carters’ inaugural with the World’s Greatest Jazz Band. And it was a Duke Ellington band, it wasn’t the real band, it was like the band after the band after the band. As a matter of fact while we were performing for Jimmy Carter I guess it was, they had a fist fight in the band.
In Duke’s band and God knows what. And the clarinet player comes to me after the thing and he says, “how do you finger a high G?” And I showed him I mean. But certainly Mr.
